title: Your First Embroidery Hoop, Finished in One Evening
dek: The supplies, the stitches worth learning first, and a small first hoop that is easy to finish in an evening.

body.text: Six stitches are enough to start. Learn them on one small hoop and you can draw a daisy, your initials or a wobbly mug in thread. It's portable, quiet and fits in a tote bag.

A kit bundles a hoop, thread, fabric and a pattern, which takes the guessing out of the first project. Loose supplies let you choose your own colors. If you're unsure, a small kit is a sensible first purchase; if you already own scissors and a scrap of cotton, loose supplies let you use what you have.

essentials: A few skeins of cotton embroidery floss in colors you like
Embroidery needles, which have a medium-to-long eye for threading several strands
A piece of cotton fabric, such as evenweave cotton, bigger than the hoop
optional: A water-soluble pen or a pencil for drawing the design
A thread organizer or a few bobbins
A needle minder, a magnet that keeps your needle from vanishing into the sofa

body.text: You probably own scissors, a pencil and a scrap of plain cotton from an old tea towel or shirt. A good small pair of embroidery scissors is a worthwhile upgrade.

body.title: Running stitch
body.note: In and out along a line. The simplest stitch to begin with.

body.title: Backstitch
body.note: Each stitch goes back to meet the last, making a continuous solid line. It is useful for outlines.

body.title: Stem stitch
body.note: Straight stitches staggered beside one another, popular for lettering and outlines.

body.title: Split stitch
body.note: Each stitch splits the one before, a little like a tiny chain. It is used for outlines and for padding other stitches.

body.title: Satin stitch
body.note: Straight stitches laid side by side to fill a shape with smooth color. Outlining the shape first, for example with split stitch, gives a neat edge.

body.title: French knot
body.note: A small knot made by wrapping the thread around the needle, good for flower centers and texture. It takes a couple of tries, so practice on scrap first.

steps: Stretch the fabric in the hoop and tighten the screw until it is taut like a drum.
Draw a simple shape on it: a leaf, a heart, your initial.
Cut a piece of floss about as long as your arm (no more than about 50 cm, or 18 inches), and separate out the number of strands your pattern or floss label calls for, one strand at a time.
Thread the needle and tie a small knot at the end.
Backstitch along the outline, keeping stitches about the same length.
Fill the shape with satin stitch, or add three French knots for a flower.

body.text: When finished, check the floss label for care instructions before washing. Test the pen or transfer method on scrap fabric first, and follow its label.

Embroidery rewards small sessions: ten minutes while the kettle boils moves a leaf along, and a hoop left on the arm of the sofa tends to get picked up. A little pouch with the needle, a few colors and the scissors means a spare half hour doesn't begin with a search.

Before committing to a full pattern, spend an evening stitching a row of each stitch on a scrap, one beneath the other. It becomes a tiny reference sampler and shows you which stitches your hands enjoy. For a second project, trace a simple outline from something you like. Lettering is a good one, since backstitch alone does the job.
Needles are sharp, so store them in a case or a needle minder.

items: **The thread keeps tangling.** The piece is too long, or the thread is twisting. Shorten it, and let the needle dangle from time to time so it untwists.
**The fabric puckers.** Pulling stitches too tight is the usual cause. Let each stitch sit flat, and keep the fabric drum-tight in the hoop.
**The back looks messy.** It does for everyone. Keep the knots small and trim the loose ends.
